thread.title: Tesla: The Autonomy Thesis - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)

author: Trent Eady
title: Tesla: The Autonomy Thesis - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)
text:
The core argument of this article is as follows:
Several valuations of Waymo ( GOOG , GOOGL ) from mainstream analysts range from ~$120 billion to $250 billion . The logic behind these valuations applies equally well to Tesla ( TSLA ) if Tesla can demonstrate equal progress toward full autonomy. There is a realistic probability that Tesla will demonstrate meaningful progress toward full autonomy by the end of 2019, following the deployment of its new neural network computer, Hardware 3 . There is, therefore, a possibility (though by no means a certainty) that Tesla's valuation, currently around $50-60 billion, will double, triple, quadruple, or quintuple by the end of 2019 . The rest of this article will attempt to answer the following questions. Why Tesla as opposed to other companies? What is the importance of Hardware 3? Why could Tesla's valuation change by a lot relatively quickly, rather than gradually?
Photo by Flo Madernebner .
Tesla's approach to autonomy Tesla is sometimes seen as an outlier or a contrarian when it comes to autonomy, but it is not alone in its philosophy or approach. Mobileye ( INTC ) shares some key similarities. So does Pronto, a new startup founded by Anthony Levandowski. Levandowski is famous for his work on autonomy at Waymo, at Uber ( UBER ), and as an entrant in the DARPA Grand Challenge . (Waymo accused Levandowski of intellectual property theft, but a judge found many of Waymo's claims to be meritless , and the patent Waymo accused Levandowski of infringing on has been mostly invalidated . The case was settled out of court.)
Mobileye, Pronto, and Tesla have three key things in common:
The belief that lidar is unnecessary for fully autonomous driving and that lidar can't compensate for weaknesses in neural networks that use camera input.
An approach to path planning - how a car plans its movement - that relies solely or predominantly on machine learning , rather than hand-coded rules.
A roadmap to full autonomy that involves developing incrementally more advanced driver assistance products along the way.
The second commonality - using a machine learning approach to path planning - is the main focus of this article.
Path planning: From hand coding to machine learning
Waymo recently published a research paper on using supervised learning for path planning. Waymo's neural network, ChauffeurNet, imitates human driving by correlating the objects surrounding the vehicle to the actions taken by the human drivers. In so doing, the neural network learns that, for instance, human drivers decelerate and brake in front of stop signs. Waymo says that its current path planning system uses a combination of machine learning and hand-coded rules, but I have a hunch that it will continue to do R&D on approaches that solely or predominantly use machine learning.
Mobileye is openly pursuing a reinforcement learning approach to path planning, wherein a neural network learns to drive through repeated experimentation in simulation. The neural network attempts to optimize for a reward function that defines the system's goals (e.g. make it from point A to point B as quickly as possible without crashing or exceeding the speed limit by more than 10%). Mobileye has an impressive demo of the technology at 33:20 in this video:
Amir Efrati at The Information recently reported that Tesla is using supervised learning to train a path planning neural network to imitate human Tesla drivers. As Waymo describes in its paper on ChauffeurNet, this does not require uploading sensor data to Tesla's servers. Instead, Tesla can upload the output of the perception neural network: the network's determinations about the objects around the vehicle. That output is known as mid-level representations. By uploading the mid-level representations data and data about the steering wheel and pedal input given by drivers, Tesla can train a neural network to correlate the two and learn to imitate human driving behaviours. Mid-level representations data is a much smaller upload than sensor data, and unlike sensor data, it doesn't require manual labelling.
In its paper, Waymo suggests that supervised learning could be the key to more effective use of reinforcement learning. If supervised learning can train a neural network to imitate human drivers reasonably well, then a simulator can be populated with virtual vehicles that behave in a realistic way. That means the driving behaviours that optimize for the reward function in simulation will actually translate to the real world. So, even if supervised learning never leads to adequate path planning, it could lead to better reinforcement learning, which might, in turn, lead to adequate path planning.
AI and robotics researcher Pieter Abbeel suggests that the reward function for autonomous cars could itself be learned from human drivers, through an approach called inverse reinforcement learning . In that case, the neural network would observe human driving and attempt to derive the reward function that human drivers' actions seek to optimize for. This is potentially useful because, in practice, it can be hard to articulate an exact reward function. There is a Monkey's Paw problem: the neural network might give you exactly what you asked for, but not what you wanted. For example, OpenAI researchers defined the reward function for CoastRunners, a boat racing video game, as maximizing the player's score. This resulted in the boat steering in an endless circle, collecting respawning items that provided bonus points. So, it's not only supervised learning that is applicable; inverse reinforcement learning is a second potential use for human driving data.
I believe that machine learning will likely be the solution to path planning, not hand coding. Writing precise instructions on how to drive in a programming language is a painstaking task, and may even be an impractical solution. As I described above in the discussion of reward functions, even precisely specifying the goal you want to accomplish is a difficult task. Precisely specifying how to execute a complex, physical task is much harder. Roboticists are still working on programming robots to walk on natural terrain. Being able to do something doesn't mean you are able to say exactly how you do it. This gap between know-how and scientific or engineering knowledge is what makes hand programming a robot car to drive so difficult.
While there has been some limited success with hand programming robots to do things, the machine learning approach is bolstered by proofs of concept like ChauffeurNet and Mobileye's work on reinforcement learning, work on other robotics applications like object grasping, and successes in complex virtual environments like the video game Dota 2 .
Training on billions of miles of human driving data Sometime around April , Tesla plans to release Hardware 3, a new neural network computer with 10x as much neural network computation as its current Hardware 2 computer. New cars will be produced with the computer inside, and existing Hardware 2 cars will be retrofitted at service centres. According to Tesla's Director of AI, Andrej Karpathy, the added computation of Hardware 3 will allow Tesla to deploy much better neural networks than are running in its cars today. The amount of computation appears to be more than Mobileye plans to use, and about the same as what a Google self-driving car engineer once indicated could be sufficient.
Hardware 3 will increase what Tesla can do in terms of inference : the determinations a neural network makes in real time, running in a car. But in so doing, it will also increase what Tesla can do in terms of training . If the perception neural network's inference is better, its mid-level representations output will more accurately reflect the actual environment. This means the mid-level representations data will be more useful for training a path planning network via supervised learning.
The combination of better inference for the perception neural network and better training for the path planning neural network means that overall performance could improve significantly by the end of 2019.
Based on estimates by Lex Fridman at MIT, when Tesla's Hardware 3 fleet reaches 340,000 cars (both produced and retrofitted), the fleet will be driving at a rate of 1 billion miles per quarter, including 145 million miles on Enhanced Autopilot. This will allow Tesla to collect mid-level representations data on an unprecedented scale, potentially leading to a breakthrough in performance for path planning. Waymo's ChauffeurNet was trained on less than 110,000 miles of human driving, and Waymo vehicles have only driven about 12 million miles in the company's entire history. Only Tesla has the vehicles and drivers in place to try training a neural network on human driving data at this scale.
It's possible that this approach will fail, and that fundamental breakthroughs in machine learning will be needed before path planning becomes a tractable problem. It's also possible that Tesla's approach will lead to rapid progress on path planning. Based on work like ChauffeurNet, I personally feel optimistic.
Reaching a $120+ billion valuation Elon Musk recently reiterated his prediction that Tesla will "probably" achieve full autonomy with production hardware roughly around the end of 2019. If Tesla is indeed able to do this, then a rational valuation for the company will be some multiple of its current valuation. Perhaps as much as 10x . But this is an extraordinary claim, and Elon has confessed to chronically running behind time, even since childhood .
My conjecture is much more conservative. Analysts from RBC ( RY ), Morgan Stanley ( MS ), and Jefferies value Waymo at roughly double to quadruple Tesla's current valuation. UBS ( UBS ) pegs Waymo's value at between 1.25x and roughly double. Tesla only needs to demonstrate as much progress toward full autonomy as Waymo for these valuation models to start applying to Tesla. Once large institutional investors are convinced of this logic, Tesla's valuation will change.
If the valuation models for Waymo were to be used for Tesla, along with the assumption that outside of autonomy Tesla is worth nothing, then Tesla would be valued at between $75 billion and $250 billion. If the estimated value of autonomy were instead added to Tesla's current market cap of around $50 billion, then the valuations would range from $125 billion to $300 billion. An increase of 1.25x to 5x is possible.
Risks and uncertainties The main uncertainty with Tesla and autonomy is simply that the future of technology is unpredictable. Conclusive information about whether a technology will work can only be obtained after a technology is developed and tested. Once a technology is developed and tested, it is no longer in the future, but in the past and present. So future technologies will always carry uncertainty. AI is particularly fraught with uncertainty since we have very little in the way of theories that predict or explain neural network performance.
One problem that could grind progress on full autonomy to an indefinite halt is if it turns out that competent driving requires a level of understanding of the world and human psychology that only humans can possess. If predicting the behaviour of drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians requires theory of mind , autonomy is hopeless. If navigating complex physical situations requires sophisticated visual question answering , then AI can't solve that problem.
A competitive risk for Tesla would be if Waymo were able to make some fundamental breakthrough in neural network performance that obviated the usefulness of higher quantities of training data. I am skeptical of this scenario because, even conceding that Waymo has access to far more AI researchers, research in AI seems to proceed in small steps distributed among the AI research community. Radical breakthroughs spearheaded by just one company or academic team are rare.
On the opposite end of the spectrum, another competitive risk comes from Mobileye. If, through its large customer base, Mobileye is able to collect much a much larger quantity of mid-level representations data than Tesla, this would negate the thing that makes Tesla unique. However, 1) if Mobileye is doing this, it's keeping it secret and 2) even if Mobileye developed full autonomy, it could take years to get it into cars at scale since this would require deploying new hardware. Tesla can just do an over-the-air update.
One advantage of lidar is that it makes it easier to detect unknown objects. With cameras, a neural network has to be trained on many images of an object before it can detect objects of that class. As a rule of thumb, you would ideally like to train on at least 1,000 images of objects from a certain class in order to recognize it at a high rate. But that's the key. If an object class is so rare that Tesla isn't able to obtain 1,000+ examples of it, then it also so rare that it probably isn't causing many accidents. If a robotic car is even slightly better at not crashing into common objects like cars, bikes, and people, but much worse at not crashing into super rare objects like watermelon carts, that's probably a good trade-off.
Costs associated with Hardware 3 Some observers may be concerned that Tesla will suffer onerous costs in developing Hardware 3, producing it for new cars, or retrofitting it in existing cars. I can put this concern to rest. (If you aren't concerned about that, feel free to skip this final section.)
On Tesla's Q3 2018 earnings call , an update on Hardware 3 was provided by Pete Bannon, a former chip designer at Apple ( AAPL ) and currently Tesla's Director of Hardware Engineering. Bannon said:
The Hardware 3 design is continuing to move along. Over the last quarter, we've completed qualification of the silicon, qualification of the board. We started the manufacturing line, qualification of the manufacturing line. We've been validating the provisioning flows in the factor. We built test versions of Model S, X and 3 in the factory to validate all the fit and finish of the parts and all the provisioning flows.
So we still have a lot of work to do. And the team is doing a great job, and we're still on track to have it ready to go by the end of Q1.
This implies that some significant proportion of the total R&D cost for Hardware 3 has already been incurred in Q3 and previous quarters, although some remains for Q4 and Q1. The cost of designing a custom chip is estimated at somewhere around $50 million per year or an average of $12.5 million per quarter. Tesla spent between an average of $355 million per quarter on R&D over the seven quarters from Q1 2017 to Q3 2018. Even if Tesla's costs for Hardware 3 were $25 million per quarter, that would still be just 7% of its average R&D spending. Ongoing Hardware 3 development (and possible future computer hardware development) will, therefore, incur a manageable R&D expense.
The unit cost of Hardware 3 is expected to be about the same as Hardware 2. This was Elon's comment on the Q3 call:
...it costs about the same. Cost, volume and power consumption are approximately the same as the current hardware...
So, the production costs of Tesla's vehicles should not be greatly impacted by the introduction of Hardware 3.
Tesla may eventually have to retrofit up to 550,000 Hardware 2 vehicles with Hardware 3. (I get this figure by taking the 280,000 estimated Hardware 2 cars on the road as of the end of Q3 and assuming, quite aggressively, an average production rate among Models S, X, and 3 of 9,000 vehicles per week from October to May.) Owners are only eligible for the upgrade if they buy the Full Self-Driving Capability software package. Until it was made unavailable for purchase , the package cost $3,000 for customers who ordered it with their car. For customers who bought the package after taking delivery of their car, as of June 27, 2018, the price was $5,000 , up from $4,000 previously. Elon has also indicated the price will be increased to $5,000 when the software package is reintroduced.
My hunch is that the software package has always been priced to exceed the cost of potential future hardware upgrades. Tesla will certainly have the freedom to price it that way when the package is reintroduced. So, any financial risk exists only with customers who already bought the software.
I estimate somewhere around 305,000 Hardware 2 cars were produced by the time the software package was made unavailable. According to one survey , 15% of Model 3 owners bought the Full Self-Driving Capability package. Among Model S and X owners, the rate might be closer to 40% . The weighted average of those two estimates is 32% (assuming 1/3 of Hardware 2 cars as of late October were Model 3, and 2/3 were S and X). That means 97,600 customers may have purchased the software (and the right to a free hardware upgrade) at $3,000.
Even if the hardware costs as much as $2,500 and the shipping and labour for the retrofit costs as much as $500 (which implies an implausibly high wage for Tesla's service technicians), the retrofits will still net out to a break-even for the Full Self-Driving Capability option. Upgrading these 97,600 vehicles would, in that case, require $293 million in cash. What this would ultimately mean is that, in effect, Tesla borrowed $293 million in cash from 97,600 of its customers, and then repaid it interest-free in the form of goods and services. The "repayment" would begin in Q2 2019. For reference, Tesla had $881 million in positive free cash flow in Q3 2018. In Q2 2019, I believe Tesla will be in a good position to "repay" this "loan".
